## What This Guide Measured That the Literature Would Want

**Strength discipline, stated before the list and not relaxed inside it.** Everything below is *measured here*, never *novel*. This chapter ran no systematic prior-art search, and several items are almost certainly known to the arithmetic community in some form. What the guide can honestly claim is that it **measured** these things, in this format, at this operand count, with reproducible artifacts, and **could not find them stated with numbers** in the sources fetched here. Both halves are required, and adjacent sources are named.

| # | measured here | where | adjacent literature, and what it does not supply |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | the price of Class III composition at *n* = 4 in binary32, split by exponent regime, against an exact single-rounding oracle — with the warning that the figure moves with how "clustered" is constructed | clause S3; ch10, "Accuracy Against the Correctly Rounded Sum" | entry 62 classifies the architectures and asserts the direction; entry 30 bounds summation error asymptotically. Neither gives a measured miss rate for a specific four-input binary32 composition |
| 2 | **"both orders agree" is a false oracle** — a substantial fraction of clustered quadruples on which tree and sequential agree bit-for-bit still miss the correctly rounded sum | ch10, "'Both Orders Agree' Is Not an Oracle" | nothing fetched here addresses it. A **verification** result rather than an arithmetic one, falsifying a cheap oracle a practitioner reaches for first — in this writer's judgement the guide's most transferable finding |
| 3 | the composed `inexact` flag over-reports one-directionally: composition can raise it when the final bits land exact, and provably never misses a genuinely inexact sum | ch10, "Flags Under Composition" | entry 65's rule that `augmentedAddition` "signals inexact only when roundTiesToZero(x + y) overflows" — a different answer to the same question, from the specification side |
| 4 | a binary32 adder can never raise the underflow flag — carried into clause S4 as an omission *with a proof* | ch07, "The Flags an Adder Can Actually Raise" | the lemma is Sterbenz's and the guide says so. The guide's own part is the claim about the *flag*, for *this* operation. **Format-specific — the retargeting section refuses to generalise it** |
| 5 | port order is part of the arithmetic specification: one operand multiset yields three classes of answer depending on **both** tree shape and port mapping, all six orders enumerated and pinned | ch10, "One Multiset, Three Answers"; clause S1 | published multi-operand papers specify the operation. Entry 81 found the analogous thing on real silicon — largest-first accumulation, an ordering the vendor never documented |
| 6 | the rounding-carry renormalise is unreachable by random stimulus — zero occurrences in a million random pairs | ch08, "Round, and the Renormalize Random Never Finds" | a quantified **verification blind spot** in the most-tested operation in computing; a null result with a stated sample size, which is the right form for one |
| 7 | a coverage model is a testbench and needs the same mutation discipline — every bin definition re-implemented independently, and the guard still let two mutations survive until the *library* was fixed | ch12, "Pinning the Bins: The Last Unpaid Debt" | ch13 confirmed against IEEE 1800-2017's coverage clause and entry 28 that stock functional coverage has **no mechanism at all** for verifying bin definitions against a second implementation |
| 8 | `!=` silently passes an undriven design, making the central equivalence sweep vacuous unless it uses `!==` with an X-guard | ch09 | almost certainly folklore somewhere, but the guide has the falsifying run |
| 9 | neither tree nor sequential is systematically more accurate at *n* = 4: per-regime differences are real but their *direction flips between regimes* | ch10 | kills the folklore that trees are "more accurate" at this width. **Keep ch10's own correction visible:** its review measured one regime's gap at >13σ, so "statistically indistinguishable" was withdrawn as an overclaim — a withdrawal that advertises the method better than the finding does |
| 10 | the reduced-width exhaustive method with its census and its limits — 65,536 pairs at E4M3, a subnormal-involvement rate an order of magnitude above random binary32's, all class crosses guaranteed, and no coverage of width-dependent bugs | ch05, "Verifying Floating Point Specifically" | plus the **E4M3 naming caveat**, cashed out above into a 1.87× difference in maximum value between two formats of one name |
| 11 | **`fp32_add4` is monotonic over 396,225 one-ulp increases — and monotonicity is a weak property**, since six of nine deliberately wrong adders pass the check unharmed | new here; `src/ch14/` | entries 81 and 62 demonstrate non-monotonicity in a deployed five-operand accumulator and generalise it to *n* ≥ 4 without intermediate normalisation. **Both halves of the row are the result** |

### Two experiments this chapter did not run

Named, because leaving them unnamed would be the same failure as claiming them. **The composition price at reduced width:** chapter 5's E4M3 machinery exists and a four-operand E4M3 sweep is 2³² quadruples — hours, not a research programme — and it would test the plausible-but-unmeasured expectation that narrower formats pay *more* for per-stage rounding. **A proof rather than a sweep for monotonicity:** the argument is three lines and is written out above; checking it formally, or going exhaustive in a reduced-width format where exhaustive is affordable, would upgrade a measurement into a theorem.

## Traps Beginners Fall Into

Every chapter has closed with the ways its own subject goes wrong. This chapter's subject is reading and citing other people's work.

**Treating an HTTP 200 as a verification.** It produced four false greens in this chapter's own bibliography, by three mechanisms — an off-host redirect to a search page, a cookie-consent landing page, and a bot interstitial served as `text/html` in place of a PDF. Check what arrived, not what the status line said: substring-test quotations against the fetched bytes, and confirm a PDF's first four bytes are `%PDF`.

**Treating a 403 as a dead link.** Six hosts refused this machine while being healthy on the open web, and one answered a *different* fetch path on the same machine in the same minute with a 200. The two paths disagree in both directions — `github.com` one way, `hal.science` the other — so a one-tool re-verification produces false failures whichever tool you picked.

**Quoting a format name without a standardising body.** "E4M3" names two formats that share field widths and differ by 1.87× in maximum value and by twelve NaN encodings. The same trap waits under "FP8", "TF32", and every posit paper published before March 2022, when the exponent field stopped being variable.

**Repeating a vendor's approximate phrasing as an exact one.** "The same dynamic range as FP32" is what a reader remembers; "the same *exponent range*" is what is true. Vendors are usually careful — the bfloat16 article says "approximate" — and the looseness gets added downstream, by people summarising.

**Citing the DOI you constructed rather than the one you resolved.** An unfollowed DOI is a guess with a respectable prefix. Two DOIs here resolve to publisher landing pages returning **202** and no document, which is why neither is asserted as the source's URL — both appear in their entries only as the record of what was tried. One resolves cleanly and is cited as such. The difference is entirely observational.

**Letting a format-specific proof travel.** Chapter 7 proved a binary32 adder can never raise the underflow flag and chapter 12 omitted the flag on that authority. The premise is a relationship between precision and subnormal ramp depth, and both move with the format.

**Measuring a weak property and reporting it as a strong one.** This chapter's own measurement is the example: monotonicity over 396,225 one-ulp increases sounds like a correctness certificate and certifies almost nothing, since six of nine deliberately wrong adders passed it. The number is worth having *with* the mutation table beside it, or it will be misread — including by whoever wrote it.

**Assuming a documentation URL is stable.** The Transformer Engine FP8 primer was reorganised and retitled between one reference to it and the next. Pin the version when the vendor offers one and quote from the pinned copy — or accept that the quotation has an expiry date you will not be told about.

## What You Should Be Able to Do Now

Check each box against the shipped material — `src/ch14/` and the bibliography — rather than from memory.

- [ ] Name the four architectural classes of multi-term adder, say which one `fp32_add4` belongs to, and give the reason from the class definition rather than from this chapter's assertion.
- [ ] Derive the 277-bit exact span of a binary32 value and the 280-bit accumulator for four addends from the field widths alone — then check your 554 and 4196 against the published table that has them.
- [ ] State the two roads out of clause S10, and say which costs a tenfold datapath and which costs an output port and a rounding direction.
- [ ] Explain why `augmentedAddition` cannot be a mode switch on this design, naming both reasons; and say why gradual underflow is a precondition rather than a preference.
- [ ] Run the `census` model above and confirm it agrees with chapter 5's published E4M3 numbers and with NVIDIA's 448 and 57,344.
- [ ] Explain, in field-layout terms, why bfloat16's dynamic range is "approximately" binary32's, and name the two places the approximation lives.
- [ ] Say why "E4M3" is not a format name without an owner, and give the two numbers that differ.
- [ ] Run the posit decoder and reproduce Table 1's fraction-length row for the two enumerable precisions (posit8 and posit16; posit32's entry is derived from the field layout, not enumerated); then explain why the taper crosses binary32's precision at 2²⁰ and point at the independent source naming the same threshold.
- [ ] Give both sides of the posit hardware-cost disagreement, attribute each, and explain why this project cannot settle it.
- [ ] `grep` `src/ch09` and `src/ch12` for `parameter` yourself, say what chapter 5's retargeting plan would actually cost, and read chapter 5's dated correction under "Verifying Floating Point Specifically" to see the guide record its own unkept promise.
- [ ] Name the four modules that carry the format, and say which one OCP E4M3 breaks hardest and why.
- [ ] Explain why a tensor core's five-operand accumulator is about the same width as this guide's two-operand one, using the taxonomy rather than a coincidence.
- [ ] Run `bash run_all.sh ch14` and account for every field of the census line — including why 70 % of one-ulp increases move nothing, and what `NaN-born` counts.
- [ ] Break the bench three ways and predict each outcome before running: `-DNT=0`, one directed vector removed, and `ordkey`'s negative branch changed from `~v` to `v`.
- [ ] Read the mutation table in `src/ch14/README.md` and answer the question it is really asking: why did the *directed vectors* catch eight of nine mutants, and what does that say about the property the bench is named after?
- [ ] Take any three URLs from the bibliography, re-fetch them, and record what you get — including which of the three lied to you about its status code.

And one habit worth carrying out of this chapter, because it is method rather than content. Every claim above about someone else's work took three steps: fetch the source, extract its text mechanically, test the quotation as a literal substring. That is about a minute per quotation. Eighty-six sources is an afternoon, and at the end of it the difference between what you believe a source says and what it says is a table you own. This guide did that in chapter 2 for the language, chapter 4 for waveforms, chapter 5 for assertions, chapter 13 for the SystemVerilog transition, and here for the literature — and every time, the table disagreed with the received account in at least one place that mattered.

## The Arc, and Where to Go Next

This is the end of the book, so it is worth saying what the book was.

Fourteen chapters ago it started with gates and truth tables and one full adder drawn badly enough that a mechanical column audit had to be invented to catch it. It ends with a pipelined, specified, proven four-input IEEE 754 binary32 adder, a verification kit whose every component has been seen to fail, and a bibliography whose every link carries a fetch status and a date. Between those two points, almost nothing was taken on authority.

That is the actual shape of the arc, and it is not "we built an adder". It is: **at every step, the guide asked what would falsify the claim, and then went and tried it.**

Chapter 2 compiled forty throwaway modules and found the folklore about `1 << 40` is wrong under context-determined widths. Chapter 3 asked how many of the fourteen classic beginner bugs the simulator reports and found the answer was one — and that races here are perfectly reproducible, so the standard advice to re-run and see never reveals one. Chapter 4 found a shipped testbench printing PASS against a design rebuilt with a missing flip-flop, and the project acquired the rule that has governed every chapter since: **no check ships until it has been seen to fail.** Chapter 5 turned that into machinery and discovered, in its own headline measurement, that re-seeding per trial had corrupted the number. Chapter 7 measured that a binary32 adder can never raise the underflow flag, so chapter 12 could omit it with a proof instead of a shrug. Chapter 8 wrote an invariant, ran a million pairs, and watched the sweep falsify it. Chapter 9 found that `!=` silently passes an undriven design, which would have made the central equivalence sweep vacuous. Chapter 10 killed the folklore that adder trees are more accurate, and showed that two structures agreeing proves nothing about either. Chapter 11 quantified how often an injected X quietly disappears. Chapter 12 retired the project's one outstanding debt with a proof, an attack, and a witness on a wire no output could reveal — then found its own coverage-bin guard had let two mutations through until the *library* was fixed. Chapter 13 audited a language and found much of what the textbooks teach is a parse error here, and a smaller, meaner fraction is accepted and silently does nothing.

This chapter did the same to the literature. Ninety-seven fetches, three mechanisms by which a 200 lies, two fetch paths disagreeing in opposite directions, one arithmetic standard readable for free and one not readable at all — and one measurement, because the fetched papers asked a question this guide's artifact was the right shape to answer.

**What a reader can do now that they could not at chapter 1.** Read an IEEE 754 bit pattern by hand and say what it is. Write a Verilog module that means what it says, and know which traps the compiler will not warn about. Build a testbench that can fail, and prove it can by breaking the design. Compose two correct units and know that composition is a specification decision, not a wiring convenience. Pipeline something without inventing an arithmetic bug in the reset. Write a specification down before verifying against it, and notice when a disagreement is really a specification dispute. And — this chapter's addition — read a paper, a standard and a vendor manual while keeping straight which of the three you are quoting.

**Where to go next**, in rough order of how well the guide has prepared you:

- **Parameterise the adder.** The guide argued for reduced-width exhaustive verification in chapter 5 and then did not do it, and chapter 5 now says so in its own text. `EXP_W` and `MANT_W` through nine files, an exhaustive E4M3 sweep as the oracle with the census above as the pinned expectation, then binary16 overnight. The exercise the guide most clearly earned and most clearly owes.
- **Run the two experiments named above** and not run here.
- **Build a Class II three-term adder.** Tenca's problem — tracking bits shifted out during alignment — is chapter 8's sticky bit with one more operand. The smallest real step toward single rounding, and you now have all the parts.
- **Get a simulator this environment does not have.** Chapter 13's Tier-3 layer is unlocked by tooling, not by knowledge.
- **Get a synthesis tool.** Every sentence in this guide about area, Fmax and timing is flagged as documentation, in eleven chapters, on purpose. That wall is a tooling wall. Knock it down and re-run chapter 11's claims.
- **Read entries 62, 65, 78, 80 and 81, in that order.** They are the five sources that would most change how you think about what chapters 8 through 12 built, and all five were fetchable from an ordinary machine on an ordinary day.

The adder is finished. The bibliography is checked. The last thing this guide has to say is what it has been saying since chapter 4, and it applies to citations exactly as it applies to testbenches: **what would have to be true for this to be wrong, and have you gone and looked?**

## Sources for This Chapter

**The annotated bibliography above is this chapter's source list**, and the guide's. Every previous chapter closed with a short section here; this one closed with eighty-seven numbered entries in the middle instead, because consolidating them was the deliverable rather than a formality. What belongs here is the record of the verification pass, so it can be reproduced rather than trusted.

**The fetch pass.** 97 distinct URLs requested from this machine on **2026-08-21**, each with `curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\t%{url_effective}' -L --max-time 40`, recording the *final* status after redirects and the effective URL beside the requested one: **79 → 200, 9 → 403, 4 → 202, 1 → 418, 1 → 429 (200 on immediate retry), 1 → 404, 2 → TLS connection reset with no status.** Every 403 was retried through a second fetch path before being written down, and where the paths disagreed both results are recorded in the entry.

**The content pass.** Sixteen sources carry quotations here. For each, the bytes were downloaded, converted to text — HTML by tag-stripping and entity-unescaping, PDF with `pypdf` — and every quoted string confirmed by a literal substring test after normalising whitespace, PDF hyphen-splits and ligatures. Three misspellings survive and are marked `[sic]`: "representatio" in the FP8 abstract, "a 33% speed improvements" in the augmented-operations abstract, and "absorbe" in the Kulisch-accumulator preprint. Two extraction artifacts are recorded where they matter: the posit standard's text layer drops inter-word spaces, and its `16n` is set in mathematical italic.

**The audit pass.** All 33 external URLs shipped in chapters 1-13 were extracted with `grep` and re-requested. **Zero dead links**, for the second time in two independent passes on the same day.

**The arithmetic.** Every census number, accumulator width and posit taper figure above was computed here under `python3` 3.11.15 by the models shown in place, from field widths alone. They reproduce chapter 5's published E4M3 census, NVIDIA's two FP8 maxima, the posit standard's Table 1, and Uguen and de Dinechin's Table 1 — none of which any model was told about.

**The one measurement.** `src/ch14/tb_mono4.v`, under Icarus Verilog 13.0 (stable, `v13_0`) with `vvp` 13.0 on Linux x86-64, reproducible with `bash run_all.sh ch14`. The mutation record, the required-failure record and the headline run are in `src/ch14/README.md`. The full repository regression stands at **123/123** under `SIM_TIMEOUT=120`, of which this chapter contributes one target and no new RTL.

**And the standing wall.** `which verilator` returns nothing on this machine, no synthesis tool is installed, and no waveform viewer can render headlessly. Every area, latency, power and Fmax figure in this chapter therefore belongs to the authors of the paper it came from and is attributed on the spot — chapter 11's "Timing, Fmax, and the Epistemic Wall", honoured one last time.
